summary: Mars WonderLab is a first-person browser game by Blue Moon that invites children ages 7–12 to manage a Martian outpost over five days. Players explore the habitat, scan equipment, repair systems and make choices about life support, power, food, radiation shelter and delayed communication with Earth. Only three supplies—Power, Air and Food—keep the decisions understandable, with costs shown before committing and consequences carried into later days. Archived NASA records shape the experience: JPL Horizons sets communication delay, and Curiosity radiation observations inform a clearly labelled, simplified shelter rule. HiRISE terrain, a Perseverance rover exhibit and NASA science cards connect exploration to real missions. Prediction questions, visible changes and a final reflection encourage players to explain their choices and try another approach. The working desktop prototype is publicly playable, with four historical scenarios and three possible endings. It aims to make engineering trade-offs tangible; learning outcomes still need testing with children.
details:
WHAT WE BUILT

Mars WonderLab is a playable, first-person desktop browser game by Blue Moon for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Children ages 7–12 explore a fictional outpost near Jezero Crater and manage a five-day mission. The experience is in English and uses mouse and keyboard.

HOW IT WORKS

The player walks between life support, greenhouse, communications, power and shelter areas, using a scanner, repair helper and tablet. A map, contextual prompts and the fictional guide ECHO support exploration. Power, Air and Food are the three abstract supplies. Important decisions show costs and expected consequences before confirmation; the effects carry into later days. Reading and walking do not consume supplies.

The mission connects five topics: producing breathable air, caring for crops, repairing the relay and power systems, preparing radiation shelter, and planning around delayed messages from Earth. Fully repairing the relay opens a later option to wait for an Earth repair procedure, creating a trade-off between local action and limited work time. Plants, lights and equipment displays reflect choices. Prediction questions, explanations, a final reflection and replay comparisons invite children to describe what they learned. Four historical NASA scenarios lead to recovery, departure-readiness or standby outcomes; the game does not simulate a rocket launch.

REAL NASA RECORDS, CLEAR GAME RULES

JPL Horizons light-time values set one-way Earth–Mars signal delays of 16–22 minutes across the selected dates. Curiosity RAD detector records from 2017, 2021, 2022 and 2024 inform one or two shelter intervals through an explicitly invented training rule: the span between the first and last readings above 1.5 times the selected-window median is compared with one Mars day. Lower readings and gaps may occur within that span. This is not a human radiation-dose estimate, a measurement at our fictional Jezero outpost, or a safe-shelter recommendation.

DONKI provides separate solar-event context. MOXIE's archived oxygen-production record supports the life-support lesson, while OSDR study OSD-267 provides the 33-day lettuce-growth example: crops do not instantly become meals during this mission. HiRISE elevation and imagery form the surrounding Jezero landscape, with a disclosed fictional flat construction pad. A credited NASA Perseverance model is a static, scannable exhibit. NASA science cards and a Jezero panorama provide optional discoveries. Archived Perseverance microphone audio is adapted into outdoor ambience.

All observations are archived, not live. The crew, story, weather effects, resource blocks and their costs are simplified or invented. Source links and explanations are available in the game. The aim is to make engineering trade-offs tangible and encourage curiosity about real missions, without presenting the game as a scientific or medical simulator.

TOOLS AND DEVELOPMENT

Built with JavaScript, Three.js/WebGL, Vite, HTML and CSS, with procedural 3D assets, quality settings, reduced-motion support and local browser saves. The public build is hosted on ChatGPT Sites. It uses embedded records and deterministic game rules; no live AI model or NASA API is required during play.

CURRENT STATUS AND NEXT VALIDATION

The publicly playable prototype includes 33 scenes, four archived scenarios, three endings and local save/replay. Automated checks cover 69,648 reachable campaign states and 81 walking routes; the production build passes. These checks do not establish educational effectiveness. Child playtesting, an unaided full human playthrough and target-device performance review remain open. The draft resource record is still being completed: the team-supplied menu track and redistributed system-voice output need their rights confirmed before final submission. A final public presentation/video link is pending.
